title: IAM Users & Groups 👥
description: Create identities for people and organise them logically.

slides.title: IAM User: A Named Identity 🧑
slides.content:
# One Person, One User

An IAM user represents a single person or a system (like a CI/CD pipeline). Each user has:
- A friendly name (like `alice`).
- An optional password for console access.
- Optional access keys (access key ID + secret access key) for programmatic access (CLI, SDK).
- Permissions (attached policies or group membership).

**Best practice**: Create one IAM user per human. Never share credentials.

slides.title: See it: Creating a User (Console vs CLI)
slides.content:
# Console and CLI Methods

In the console, you can create a user with a few clicks. Using the AWS CLI, you’d run:
slides.codeSnippet:
aws iam create-user --user-name alice
aws iam create-login-profile --user-name alice --password 'TempP@ss123' --password-reset-required

slides.title: IAM Groups: Organise Users 📁
slides.content:
# Apply Permissions to Many Users at Once

Instead of attaching policies to individual users, you can create **groups** and add users to them.
- Group `Developers` might have access to EC2 and S3.
- Group `Admins` gets full access (but still not root).

A user can belong to multiple groups. Permissions from all groups are **cumulative** (the union of all policies).

**Note**: Groups are not a true identity – you can’t be logged in “as a group”. They’re purely permission containers.

quizData.question: Why are IAM groups recommended over attaching policies directly to each user?

options.text: It’s easier to manage permissions at scale
Users can’t have policies directly attached
Groups provide an extra layer of encryption

quizData.explanation: Groups let you update permissions for many users at once, following the principle of least privilege without repetitive work.

slides.title: How Permissions Are Evaluated ⚖️
slides.content:
# The Union Logic

When a user tries to do something, AWS evaluates **all** policies attached to:
- The user directly
- Any group the user belongs to
- (Later) Any role the user assumes

If **any** policy allows the action, and **no** explicit deny blocks it, it’s allowed. An explicit deny in any policy overrides all allows.

This is the **default deny → explicit allow** model.

slides.title: ⚠️ Beware of Over‑permission
slides.content:
## Don’t Give * Wildcard

It’s tempting to attach `AdministratorAccess` to everyone. That defeats the purpose. Start with minimum permissions (least privilege) and add only what’s needed.
